title: The Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16–30)
hookLine: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom to captives

cards: After the desert, Jesus comes back to Galilee, and word about him spreads. Then he goes home to Nazareth, where he was brought up. On the Sabbath he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom.
These people watched him grow up and know his family. He stands up to read, the attendant hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaias, and he unrolls it and finds the place he's looking for.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT OF THE LORD IS UPON ME.
teach.b: He reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor."
And on: to heal the contrite of heart, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord.
Anointed is the root of the title Christ: Christos, the anointed one, in Hebrew Messiah.

The acceptable year echoes the jubilee in the law of Moses, when land went back to its families and those sold into service went free. Then he rolls up the scroll and sits down, the posture of a teacher.
Every eye is on him. And the sermon Luke gives us is one sentence: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." At first they marvel at his gracious words.
Then someone says: isn't this Joseph's son?

Jesus answers that no prophet is accepted in his own country, and reminds them of two old stories we read a few weeks ago: Elias was sent not to the widows of Israel but to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon; Eliseus healed not the lepers of Israel but Naaman the Syrian.
God's blessing, going to outsiders. The hometown crowd is filled with anger, and they drive him to the brow of the hill to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.

teach.h: THIS DAY IS FULFILLED THIS SCRIPTURE.
teach.b: Luke puts this near the start of the ministry, and some readers hear it as a program for all that follows: good news for the poor, and a welcome wider than anyone expected.

how: Catholics hear Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass of Holy Week, when the bishop blesses the holy oils, and on a Sunday in Ordinary Time in the year of Luke's Gospel.

games.q: in the Nazareth synagogue — tap the pairs.

s: Luke records a long sermon after the reading
Luke gives it as one sentence: this day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears.
the crowd turned angry when Jesus spoke of the widow of Sarepta and Naaman
God's blessing going to outsiders, and they drove him to the brow of the hill.
Jesus read from the scroll of the prophet Jeremias
it was the scroll of Isaias.

games.q: you're in the Nazareth synagogue. the carpenter's son has just read Isaiah, said it's fulfilled today, and reminded you that God once blessed a foreign widow and a Syrian general. what does the crowd do?
o: ask him for the miracles he did in other towns, and wait politely.
fill with anger and drive him to the brow of the hill.
games.why: they're filled with anger and try to throw him down. but he, passing through the midst of them, went his way.

practice: Find Luke 4:18 and read it aloud, slowly, the way Jesus did in the synagogue, or just say the phrases: good news to the poor, healing for the brokenhearted, deliverance to captives, sight to the blind, liberty for the bruised.
Let each phrase land on a real person you know: someone poor, someone heartbroken, someone stuck. If you pray, hold each of them before God.

wordCard.voice: Christos. Greek for the anointed one: the title's root, read aloud by Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue the day he said this scripture is fulfilled. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: he has anointed me, Luke 4:18; from chrio, to anoint, the root of Christos, the anointed one.

carryVoice: Your line: good news to the poor. The first words of his work, read aloud at home. Day four hundred fifty-one, done.
